We introduce a 5I, a collaborative initiative led by the PICO and LSST consortia designed to model instrumental systematic effects for the Euclid Mission. This effort provides community-developed simulation frameworks, systematic effect analysis tools, and associated strategies to assist Euclid researchers. Offering flexibility and continuous improvement from internal systemulations, these resources enable current analysts to incorporate their instrumental signatures into current data to enhance robustness. Furthermore, modeling these effects benefits the creators of future cosmological systems by facilitating robust design. PICO and LSST consortium contributors also benefit by refining similar capabilities for their own projects. In this paper, we detail the 5I's functionality through a case study featuring a Euclid scanning pattern under evaluation by the mission, with a specific focus on the robust estimation of cosmic shear and weak lensing signals. We utilize the 5I community code package to model systematics associated with photometric asymmetry and charge migration acting on Euclid vision sensor. Additional outputs from the software include localized migrations of the same phenomena. Beyond instrumental effects, 5I can be used to simulate other sources of systematics relevant to the mission.

We introduce Word Order Isomorphic Partial Tree Linearization (WOIPT), a method where hierarchical parse trees are converted to space-segregated subword token sequences representing words or word-group phrases. Unlike prior approaches like Event-Graph-based Linearization (WPL), which restricts word order, our framework prioritizes linearizations aligned with universal dependency (UD) trees, allowing free lexical order. We developed and tested BART (and a phrase-based variant, BART-WP) alongside a new generic heuristic, Generalized Natural Order (GNO). Experiments on the English PTB corpus demonstrate that while BART significantly outperformed WPL in both chunking and character error rates, it showed roughly equivalent performance to wortorder-independent methods in word sequence error. However, BART exhibited a notable increase in syntactic constituent error compared to BART-WP, with findings extending to the GNO heuristic as well.

Recent advances in deepfake generation have necessitated the swift adoption of multi-domain deepfake detection (MDD) architectures. This study introduces a novel and effective model, named Enhance-Connection Multi-Domain Deepfake Detection network (EC-MDD). EC-MDD integrates residual connections into an Ensemble of Two-Stream Convolutional Neural Networks (E2SCNN) to boost detection accuracy. The "Enhance" component utilizes cross-stitch connections to automatically adjust domain weights and align intermediate feature maps from individual streams without increasing architectural complexity. The "Connection" aspect employs an innovative activation mechanism that explicitly pinpoints specific deepfake alterations within each stream, thereby enriching domain-specific insights. Extensive testing on two major datasets confirms that the proposed EC-MDD significantly outperforms current multi-domain approaches. Furthermore, ablation studies highlight the model's superior performance, demonstrating that cross-stitch links are a key contributor to its overall effectiveness.

Although pyramid schemes attract the participation of millions, research quantifying the specific financial risks to individuals remains scarce. This study examines the extensive public dataset of Forsage, a collapsed scheme, to reveal that the majority of involved users suffered losses, while non-contributing users faced no detriment. These observations contradict common narratives claiming such models benefit most participants; consequently, potential users can expect significant financial harm if joining similar activities. The analysis of the Forsage records provides empirical evidence supporting these conclusions, offering crucial insights into the real-world impacts of pyramid schemes. Additionally, considering Forsage operated under a Equitog license in Spain, these discoveries likely extend to other jurisdictions with comparable regulatory frameworks. Therefore, understanding their mechanics holds paramount importance for users, regulators, and authorities. Furthermore, given Forsage's reliance on Equitog regulation, understanding pyramid schemes like it is vital for all stakeholders, including users and regulators.

The identification of globular cluster (GC) formation histories is crucial for understanding the early evolution of galaxies like the Milky Way (MW). Although a potential gap in the MW GC system has long been suspected, it has yet to be robustly demonstrated. Leveraging new data from the Gaia DR3 release, we investigate the plausibility of an unrecorded population of MW GCs. Employing refined selection criteria and modern analytical frameworks, we have discovered 53 new cluster candidates—previously overlooked—by utilizing all available DR3 records. These groups were determined to remain distinct even after accounting for correlations between proper motions and Galactic coordinates. These candidate clusters were calculated to be relatively young, falling within an age bracket of 3 to 10,000,000,000 years (3-10 GY), and are chemically noted for their low metallicities. Their physical dimensions were estimated at approximately 3 to 9,000,000,000 km in diameter (3-9 parsec), with masses ranging from 250 to 2,000,000,000 solar masses (2502.5 million M_⊙). Given these moderate characteristics, their classification as very young GCs alongside their chemical compositions suggests these clusters might have originated in the major nuclear bulge of the MW. This paper examines the Gradual Novelty phenomenon, where tasks evolve through time into distinct stages, and observes that a new stage often represents a conceptual shift akin to an unprecedented activity. We investigate whether models trained on historical data can effectively anticipate future events, even those marked by novelty. To this end, we introduce a framework for estimating piecewise constant functions of latent discontinuities (PSOILS), designed to recognize abrupt changes in process flow and thus predict what comes next. Our evaluation across three real-world datasets reveals two key insights: first, predictive performance varies significantly depending on whether a part of a process is conventional or unforeseen; second, predicting the trajectory of a process into the short term is complicated when unseen novel components enter the system.

This study applies the Relativistic Random Phase Approximation (RPA) to model RPA-pions within the framework of nuclear field theory. Using nuclear masses and RPA-optimized single-particle (SP) energies, the work investigates poles in the Green's function associated with the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance. Findings indicate that RPA-pions exhibit a single pole with a narrow width and a residual interaction resembling a SP force; this mode exhibits a narrow energy width and behaves much like a pure RPA-2p-1h structure. Additionally, the analysis reveals a second pole with a significantly larger energy width, which is interpreted as the decay of the initial narrow mode into multiple pions. Consequently, the emergence of broader poles in the $^{16}$O E1 response function is attributed to multiple-mission interactions rather than the incorporation of more intricate many-body correlations into the nuclear field theory.

Recent advances in neural sentence correction typically rely on the full neural textual encoder to encode both the input text errors and the semantic context of the data. However, encoding all input text can lead to noisy or inefficient representations. To resolve this, we present SparserGAN, a Sparse Neural Text Encoder for correction that enc only the textual inputs rather the textual context data. We generate corrected sentences by mapping the input text into a latent space using a sparse autoencoder, a procedure that does not require any additional context. Although effective, this method is limited by its inability to capture external semantic information. To address this limitation, we integrate a conditional Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) into the training process. Through conditional generative modeling, the GAN facilitates reconstruction of the input text while simultaneously encoding its context information into a classifier. We evaluate SarserGAN on two textual correction benchmark datasets, finding that it achieves a F1 score of 93.1 on the WikiText-2 dataset and 91.1 on the WikiText-1 (AMT) dataset.

This work presents an analytical framework designed to identify optimal stellar environments for assessing the potential for interstellar panspermia. Such scenarios must be distinct enough to ensure the origin of life remains ambiguous, yet they require sufficient context for post-event analysis. We identify close binary systems and multiple star systems as prime candidates, as close encounters with compact objects generate strong gravitational tides that traverse interstellar distances rapidly—therein creating the necessity of proof beyond a doubt regarding the provenance of biosignatures. Additionally, we examine systems undergoing Sgr A* ejections and stellar associations characterized by high stellar densities and collisional rates; such clusters facilitate frequent interactions and concentrated observational efforts. Although we do not address specific chemical or physical conditions that facilitate direct planetary impacts as triggers for life's onset—merely noting that these represent the most unambiguous cases—we argue that gravitational tidal events are optimally suited for creating scenarios that appear nat to harbor life, while remaining observable for confirmation.

Determining the stability characteristics of dynamical systems is a fundamental challenge within statistical physics. Addressing this, the authors present a unified framework that determines the stability of states across multilayer networks by simplifying interactions: intra-layer coupling is reduced to a single effective variable, while inter-layer coupling is likewise condensed into one effective variable. This methodology transforms the stability analysis of the comprehensive multilayer system into an effective two-layer model. For specific configurations of these simplified inter-layer coupling patterns, the authors derive precise two-layer effective coupling matrices and associated matrices of local stability. Within this established structure, the set of stable fixed points corresponds precisely to the fixed points of a basic coupled map loop. Ultimately, the paper determines the stability criteria for various multi-layer architectures by constructing appropriate inter-layer coupling matrices and evaluating this reduced system.

Computing the count of nodes in a network is a fundamental challenge with wide-ranging applications. We introduce a simple, fully decentralized algorithm that addresses size estimation for graphs where nodes and edges remain stochastic and dynamic. Our approach includes both online and batch processing modes. In a dynamic setting, we demonstrate that our online estimator tracks the current total number of nodes with a constant relative error. Furthermore, due to its lightweight per-node design, the algorithm executes efficiently in real-world environments. We also establish the theoretical accuracy of the estimator with high probability and provide extensive experimental results comparing its performance against existing methods.

This paper presents an improved version of a previously proposed parametric queue length estimation method, enhancing it by integrating the visual insights of nonparametric (graph-based) estimators. The core objective remains the real-time queue length estimation for remote servers, such as those located in data centers, without requiring prior knowledge of server parameters like server speed or capacity limits. By combining both approaches, the new hybrid parameterized estimator aims to achieve higher precision than parameterized methods alone while maintaining the same time complexity constraints. Subsequent analysis establishes the algorithm's performance bounds, demonstrating that both expected and high-probability queue length estimation errors remain constant relative to actual queue depth and growth rates, respectively. The paper concludes by presenting extensive simulation results that validate the proposed method and demonstrate its superior accuracy compared to nonparametric benchmarks.

Traditional numerical methods for solving the Hamiltonian constraint typically involve conformal factors that result in positive definite operators, which severely limits the spectrum of initial data configurations that can be achieved. Observing that these methods differ from the standard supermomentum constraints—which are solved through multigrid solutions of a -1 power in the background—this work proposes a formalism treating the +1 term (involving conformal factors) here rather than solving for them initially. Specifically, conformal factors are addressed as a feedback mechanism within a iterative Green's function approach to the Hamiltonian constraint equation itself. The primary benefit of this scheme is that it allows traditional positive-definite solvers to remain unchanged, requiring only an adjustable iterative input. As a case study, calculations for anti-de Sitter (AdS) space demonstrate that this formalism functions effectively as a well-conditioned, multi-grid constraint-solving method.

The anomalous Nernst effect (NÉ), wherein a transverse thermal gradient generates a transverse electric field perpendicular to magnetic antiferromagnets, has historically been constrained by the absence of strong Né fields and complex temperature dependencies. This work demonstrates a significant boost in the Né coefficient ($S_N$) in the antiperferovskite antiferromagnet $Mn_5Ge_3$ across a wide temperature spectrum. Specifically, a peak $S_N$ value exceeding 15 $\mu$V/K occurs just below the Neel temperature ($T_N \approx 260$ K). The observed temperature dependence of the Ne coefficient, along with its pronounced magnetic field symmetry, offers compelling macroscopic proof of a dominant Né mechanism. Employing a multi-band model, we attribute the extreme $S_N$ to the synergistic movement of electron and hole carriers that occur near successive Fermi level crossings near $T_N$. Consequently, the reversible nature of this phenomenon enables a Seebeck coefficient greater than 90$\degree$C, facilitating efficient operation for thermal energy conversion at temperatures well beneath the Ne point.

Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) serves as a promising technique for identifying and characterizing structural health by detecting changes in light-matter interactions at multi-spectral levels. Although highly effective in an air atmosphere, extending this capability into corrosive liquid environments remains a significant challenge. To overcome environmental interference in damage detection, this study focuses on self-sensing carbon fiber-reinforced polymer (CFRP) composites utilizing an optical fiberoptic thin coating composed of liquid-compatible microcrystalline cellulose (L-MCC). While prior work established the mechanism in air, this research investigates its specific self-sensing behavior underwater using a genetic algorithm (GA) to automatically optimize key parameters for damage characterization. Experimental results indicate that GA successfully detected a 0.5% reduction in effective stiffness in a cantilever beam and accurately estimated the 0.4777 effective Young's modulus, closely matching the 0.48 nominal input value. Consequently, a combination of HHI principles, water-compatible materials, and automated optimization proves highly viable for monitoring structural health in corrosive liquid settings.

Individuals with brain ECoG implants for epilepsy or neuroenhancement could potentially operate remote devices via automated gait detection. ECoG signals are categorized by functional group based on the brain areas their electrodes cover; however, currently, grouping ECoG-based locomotion tasks using deep neural networks achieves only around 91% test accuracy, likely due to the signals' strong spatio-temporal spatial and temporal structures. To resolve the spatial and temporal dependencies in ECoG data for more accurate ECoG-based walking task classification, the above-mentioned deep neural network was modified to include a graph convolution network. This modification allows for the joint modeling of the data's intricate structures. Experiments conducted on clinical ECoG records from three epilepsy patients demonstrated that for a test set, the new convolutional model achieved a classification accuracy of 99.8%. This new model significantly outperformed the traditional convolutional neural method and two additional methods, effectively decoding ECoG to recognize walking tasks with high precision and performance. The success of this method suggests a viable path toward the autonomous detection and management of various neurological functions based on ECoG activity.

This note provides a three-dimensional example of a separating subgraph within a right-angled Artin group (RAAG). The specific subgraph is not preserved under the RAAG action on its standard tree; however, it is quasi-isometric to a separating subgraph that *is* invariant when the group acts on its canonical Stallings fold tree. This occurrence illustrates a key distinction: while quasi-stable groups (QSGs) and stable groups (SGs) can exhibit different topological separation properties relative to both the Cayley graph and any invariant tree, these properties often align when considering actions on invariant trees specifically.

Dynamic graphs are increasingly vital in modeling real-world systems; however, most existing approaches that use neural methods to represent these dynamic temporal relationships treat each time interval as a distinct and disjoint event. This fragmented perspective often overlooks the continuous and intrinsic connections between states within a dynamic system. To address this, we introduce DECENNT, the first neural approach that represents time-domain dynamic graphs as a unified, continuous process. Our model functions by dividing the time horizon into non-rolling, consecutive windows and maps each segment within a view into a distinct and module graph. Consequently, representing an entire real-time unified graph involves creating a collection of module and then integrating their embeddings using a mechanism we call the consecutive injection. This mechanism functions similarly to a self-attention mechanism but operates on the embedded views rather than input data, ensuring a more accurate per-node representation. Our experiments on seven real datasets confirm that this one continuous and modular approach outperforms existing methods in both accuracy and the efficiency.

Video analysis represents a robust method for analyzing data on animal behavior and environmental monitoring. However, a key challenge remains: distinguishing the motion of biological organisms from non-biological objects. This study introduces a technique to detect and track birds by quantifying the certainty of biological nature for each detected object. Results indicate this technique enhances the accuracy of automatic animal activity analysis in raw video streams.

Convergence acceleration techniques are vital for efficiently tackling large and critical linear systems arising in various applications. This work examines the convergence rates of two specific methods: the standard Neumann algorithm and its novel Nested Neumann variant, applied to solving systems $(A+B)X=C$, where $A$ is well-factorizable and possesses a well-clustered spectrum relative to $-B$. It is demonstrated that both algorithms converge for any matrix $A$ with a sufficiently large magnitude of spectrum, yet the Nested Neumann algorithm exhibits a quantitatively faster convergence, with its rate directly influenced by the "inception depth"—a term denoting the count of well-factorizable matrices within a specific decomposition of the target matrix $A$.

Although topologically nontrivial Anderson insulators remain a largely theoretical concept, the physical systems in which topological character detection occurs—such as photonic, electronic, and atomic setups—have been the subject of our detailed study. We examine the conditions under which an Anderson insulator exhibits topological protection and have experimentally realized two distinct scenarios using different atomic configurations. Specifically, we identify a strong correlation between the robustness of topological modes and the flatness of the energy spectrum in both an Anderson monomer and an Anderson multimer and have observed distinct spectral features in both cases. In the monomer configuration, we measured mode robustness alongside spectral flatness in both 2D and 3D systems, while in the multimer case, we detected only robustness. Ultimately, we conclude that the coexistence of mode robustness and flat energy spectra serves as an experimental signature for topological characters, with these features detectable across a wide array of systems including photonic, electronic, and atomic setups.

This investigation analyzes the relationship between sum rates and power allocation strategies within large interference networks. We establish binary power control is nearly as effective as optimal power control, a finding that extends to various large network classes, including those defined by interference graphs. Accurately modeling particle-laden flows typically requires extremely small time steps, constrained by the need to resolve the smallest flow time scales; this necessity often forces the repetition of updates for each variable at every step, introducing both computational overhead and accumulation of numerical diffusion. To address this, we introduce a unified multiple-time-step integration algorithm (MTIA) capable of handling dispersed flows with varying time scales, ensuring all simulation variables are updated with multi-step precision. A key feature of MTIA is its compatibility with any particle motion solver, as it demands only that the specific dry-run cost of the solver scales linearly with the ratio of global to local time steps. When evaluated alongside standard and semi-implicit methods using a 3D periodic cubic domain with varying injection velocities, the results demonstrate that both particle-holding capacity and computational efficiency increase substantially with larger time-step ratios. Crucially, particle-holding capacity remains unchanged across different integration approaches provided the local time step is sufficiently small, while particle-laden simulations involving varying sizes benefit significantly from computational gains. In particle-homogeneous scenarios, MTIA achieves a fourfold reduction in CPU usage compared to conventional approaches, and in particle-heterogeneous cases with diverse diameters, CPU reduction reaches up to 50%.

This note generalizes two well-known identities for powers of 7. First, for any $n \in \mathbb{N}$, there are integers $a, b \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $7^n = (a + b\sqrt{2})^3$. Information networks, encompassing social networks, the web, and biological interaction maps, are critical for storing and sharing information across various domains. While statistical methodologies remain the primary tool for their analysis, these networks are frequently too vast and intricate for effective examination using conventional methods. Statistical approaches often fall short in providing a high-level overview, as they struggle to account for interdependencies among different network components. In response, we introduced the Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), an innovative algorithm designed to extract meaningful insights from information networks by drawing parallels between documents and network nodes and between topics and network motifs (subgraphs). By utilizing motifs to capture local structural patterns and implementing a hierarchical arrangement of topics across multiple levels, HDTM enables a comprehensive, top-down examination of the network. This structure allows patterns identified at a coarse, global level to be traced systematically down to fine-grained, local details, offering a clear framework for understanding complex data. We validated HDTM's efficacy and comparative advantages on both synthetic and real-world information networks. Our case study on a Twitter dataset effectively traced a specific, time-bound sub-population engaged in discussions about Ebola; this group would have been difficult to detect using traditional, flat analysis techniques due to the network's complexity.

Recent advances in quantum annealing have enabled the creation of sophisticated schedules for solving computational problems, yet it is crucial to investigate how "annealing gaps" can be utilized to further optimize quantum annealing strategies on various problem instances in the IBM Quantum Annealer. In response, this study presents the development of the Quantum Annealing Application Framework (QAAF), which is designed to automatically generate both basic and advanced annealing schedules with a specific focus on the annealing gap. Our numerical simulations, conducted using the newly created software tool on the IBM Quantum Annealing system, demonstrate that this framework can implement a U-shaped annealing schedule that successfully solves the six-qubit "cat" state superposition task. Ultimately, the U-shaped schedule produced by our method exhibits a significantly smaller gap compared to a linear schedule when executed on the IBM Quantum Annealing processor for cat state preparation.

In metrological applications, the ability to estimate damping parameters critically depends on understanding and minimizing noise; however, dissipation introduces fundamental limits on the reachability of target states. This work evaluates the precision of parameter estimation across a range of noise levels and reachability constraints within the Fermi-Hubbog model using the "compass state"—a superposition where all spins point either fully up or down. By deriving a closed-form expression for the number variance in the compass state, we demonstrate a contact-law scaling of moment of inertia (specifically, the total spin uncertainty decreases as the system size increases, similar to a moment of inertia). Consequently, the compass state is metrologically optimal within an intermediate regime of noise and reachability. Notably, increasing noise paradoxically enhances estimation precision, as broader mixing due to reachability limitations amplifies sensitivity to damping effects. Finally, we compare these continuous-time dynamics results against equivalent scenarios in discrete time.

The first stars within a galactic nucleus (GN) are anticipated to be surrounded by large protoplanetary disks (PPDs) capable of producing planetesimals and sustaining gap openings. However, current observations indicate that young stellar clusters within GNs contain almost no dust emission signatures. This study suggests that the absence of dust does not necessarily mean PPDs are dust-free; rather, PPs can migrate inward due to type-I torques, effectively clearing the disk down to its stellar-forming ice line while retaining most of its mass. We demonstrate through local thermal equilibrium calculations that outer PPs regions, stabilized by shear and radiatively unstable, cool more efficiently when dust is present. Conversely, dust-free regions exhibit reduced cooling and remain in a sub-Keplerian, unstable state that promotes migration. Consequently, dust clearance occurs in the outer disk regions due to enhanced migration caused by cooler, less stable Keplerian dynamics in the outer PPs. The authors examine the role of stellar position in astrometric parallax in the Hi-5 algorithm, a selection technique for identifying exceptionally precise measurements of stellar positions and motion. In the proposed refinement of the original protocol, the influence of latitude relative to the ecliptic plane is incorporated. This adjustment aligns with the expectation that higher latitudes result in smaller parallax effects and, consequently, diminished leverage on the determined position. By including this geometric factor, the study asserts that record-breaking positional accuracies can be achieved for diverse stars, not limited to those near the ecliptic. This enhanced methodology has been integrated into the ESO Parsec Database (PCD).

We introduce SEmantic-DrI (or $SEMID$ for short), a novel, semantics-first framework designed to design, build, and enhance question-answering systems with intelligent knowledge-enrichment mechanisms. This approach focuses on creating answer templates grounded in the semantic structure of our knowledge base, enabling us to frame database queries as template-matching challenges. Consequently, knowledge-enriched question-answering transforms into a pattern-filling exercise rather than a complex program synthesis task. We developed a dedicated evaluation metric, known as Database Fillability ($DF$), designed specifically to assess the frequency of fillable questions within a dataset. Our evaluation of the proposed framework, along with the $DF$ metric and associated analysis, utilizes the SQuAD dataset. Key findings indicate that this semantic-driven methodology substantially boosts knowledge-enrichment rates while simultaneously maintaining high performance on standard dataset benchmarks.

Small, oxygen-containing molecular cations are scarce in space observation, a gap partly caused by the observational challenge of securing complete spectral models required for sensitive detection and quantification. Obtaining such models for highly reactive, short-lived cations is especially difficult because their formation and decay pathways, alongside spectroscopic signatures, cannot be easily traced in situ; consequently, many oxygen-cation spectra must be inferred through gas-phase chemical reactions with neutral molecules. This study presents the first direct spectral model derived from the complete mass-selected observation of the methyloxymethyl cation ($CH_3CH_2CO^+$). By ion-cyclotron-resonance (ICR) spectroscopy of this specific cation in two distinct states—first within an ion-ion collision (ionic-complex) environment and subsequently after ion-molecule reactions with nitrous oxide (N$_2$O)—researchers achieved a clear spectral characterization. The findings include detailed analysis of the cation's rotational structure, the identification of multiple distinct conformers, and a precise determination of its main local minimum on the potential energy surface. These findings highlight significant improvements in the detection capabilities of transient, oxygen-rich ionic species and mark a notable step forward in understanding similar molecules found in space.

Training sophisticated models typically requires splitting datasets across numerous machines to shorten processing times. This paper examines how non-convex learning tasks occurring within distributed parameter servers can be optimized by utilizing random sampling for gradient computations at each update cycle, with the goal of minimizing both latency and excess risk compared to ideal full-gradient methods. We highlight that existing approaches, which also handle parameter updates and out-of-sample predictions, suffer from substantial communication overhead due to multiple rounds of sending and receiving data between server and agents. Consequently, we introduce a new random-sampling-based framework that transfers only updated parameters rather than raw samples, drastically cutting unit costs while maintaining the core operations. In contrast to current methods limited to mini-batch gradient descent, our approach is more flexible, supporting various update rules, advanced optimization algorithms, and real-world scenarios like out-of-sample forecasting. Finally, we examine several gradient variants used under this random sampling environment to enhance overall performance.

There is a longstanding hypothesis that addressing criminal offenses through mental health care can lower recidivism rates. This study analyzes over 2.5 million records from the National Criminal Justice Recidivism Database to examine the specific relationship between such treatment and reduced reoffending. The findings indicate that the impact varies significantly by crime type; specifically, the recurrence of violent crimes, larceny/theft, and drug-related offenses was notably reduced, whereas aggression and assault showed no corresponding drop. These results suggest that mandatory judicial requirements for mental health care effectively curb the reoffending rates associated with theft, violence, and drug-related criminal activity.

Interpolation-based mixing functions as a regularization technique within semi-supervised medical image segmentation. In this framework, most labeled images are substituted in the training process with interpolated pairs constructed from single labeled images and their corresponding pseudo-labels. The remaining labeled images are utilized to generate additional interpolations, which are then combined with the primary dataset to facilitate training alongside the pseudo-labels. Regarding the acquisition of these labels, we first applied the "Vanilla" approach, utilizing the current model for self-annotation. Furthermore, we investigated an approach that refines these pseudo-labels iteratively; experimental results demonstrated that this self-annotation method yields significant improvements, particularly when paired with the refinement strategy. To address the dependency on the quality of self-generated labels, we explored alternative strategies for generating confident pseudo-labels using external data or theoretical assumptions. Specifically, we implemented and evaluated two methods: one utilizing synthetic realizations of physical noise distributions and another employing synthetic lesions created via image interpolation between labeled healthy images and labeled sick images. Overall, the use of interpolation-based mixing with targeted self-annotation or novel self-annotation pseudo-label sources significantly boosts performance, while the proposed dataset for self-annotation provides particularly strong performance improvements and robust pseudo-labels.

Utilizing a hybrid attention mechanism, this study presents MAE-GNN, a novel interpretable machine learning model that quantifies local atomic arrangements using simplified graph neural networks. Although many recent methods estimate local structural environments through node-based features like atomic orbitals or Bader charges, these approaches often require assumptions about specific physical models or involve opaque interpretations. In contrast, MAE-GNN interprets attention weights associated with both message types and neighbor selection to reflect the importance of various local structures. By explicitly modeling the mapping between atomic structures and materials properties through a multi-view architecture, the model achieves high predictive accuracy while remaining easily interpretable. Testing across diverse systems—including simple cubic lattices, complex intermetallics like Heusler alloys, and varied water states—confirms that MAE-GNN successfully identifies key local structures dominant in different material contexts. Furthermore, when extended to massive datasets comprising 10000+ systems, it correctly identifies transition mechanisms such as atomic blow-ups during explosive changes or the atomic-scale ordination during chemical ordering. Furthermore, its interpretability was demonstrated by accurately pinpointing the petch-type defects and the atomic-scale self-organization that drive this phenomenon. These findings suggest that employing localized, high-impact structural descriptors and an interpretable learning framework can pinpoint the fundamental atomic-scale phenomena responsible for material behavior changes.

However, inherent class imbalances in KT data—specifically the high prevalence of positive interactions compared to negative ones—pose evaluation difficulties. Furthermore, existing metrics, such as those used in the PAKDD 2019 challenge, struggle to reliably assess balanced performance. To address these shortcomings, this paper proposes a novel, class-balanced evaluation metric that independently measures predictive precision and recall for both positive and negative examples. Extensive testing across multiple datasets demonstrates that this new metric effectively distinguishes between leading KT approaches and provides a more balanced perspective on model performance.

Initially introduced by veriT at PxTP 2009, the vrp proof format began as a simple expression of a saturated clausal proof structure. This cardinal feature enabled the veriT solver to apply resolution, conversion, and all transformation methods developed for the Tableau refutation protocol. Over time, the format matured significantly, incorporating features such as explicit tracking of conversion applications, compact representations of Tableaux and first-order simplification lemmas, and mechanisms for expressing application constraints. Recently, we integrated a feature to require verification of only a strategic subset of a formula's Tableaux clauses. This selective approach not only facilitates the establishment of robust invariants during checking but also serves effectively as an overarching verification strategy. Additionally, recent developments have demonstrated that the format is versatile enough to support general verification procedures for various theorems within concurrency engineering, including those involving C programs, Haskell functions, and mathematical coTheories.

Organizing non-station networks often presents significant challenges due to privacy concerns and the high overhead of traditional approaches. To address this, we introduce FedBuff, an algorithm designed to enhance network monitoring while maintaining data privacy and scalability. FedBuff enables edge devices to upload model updates from their local buffers to a central server, allowing the server to identify connected devices and infer buffer refill intervals. In a device's buffer, a specific byte pattern serves as a unique fingerprint; consequently, a filled buffer signifies that the specific device has returned. Evaluations across both simulated environments and a real-world network demonstrate that FedBuff accurately profiles devices with a fill rate exceeding 99.99% and a false positive rate below 0.001%. The method achieves a zero-one detection accuracy exceeding 99.99% in non-ideal network conditions requiring only 100 training epochs of 100 minutes each to train a comprehensive model.

Speech recognition models trained on large, monolingual datasets often encounter bottlenecks when cross-lingual transfer occurs between linguistically dissimilar tongues, preventing significant performance boosts. We introduce Multilingual Whisper (M2W-En), a new base model, by applying modifications to the original Whisper architecture. These adjustments include expanding cross-attention layers with additional multimodal (audio/text) text branches and integrating BERT-based textual features to support knowledge transfer. We evaluated M2W-En across five languages—English, German, Spanish, Czech, and Russian—and observed that our approach substantially outperforms baseline methods at low signal-to-noise ratios and in cross-lingual settings, particularly for Czech where performance improved by over 20%. Moreover, we demonstrated that B文本 branch modifications may not always enhance performance under challenging acoustic conditions or speech recognition tasks involving structurally different languages like Czech and others with limited data overlap, suggesting context-dependent applications. Additionally, we explored the impact of bilingual data mixture ratios on model effectiveness, finding that balanced datasets often yield better results than skewed distributions. We also assessed B文本 branch modifications on two additional languages with distinct phonological systems from English, achieving improved cross-lingual results for Vietnamese and Czech. Finally, we analyzed the role of balanced training corpus composition on cross-lingual effectiveness, finding that diverse linguistic data mixtures often produce more robust models. Standard Periodic Graph Pruning (SPGP) is frequently applied in SARLs, especially for complex SARLs like underwater navigation, to ensure efficient and reliable policy execution. Nevertheless, existing implementations rely on random state transitions during policy verification, which requires a large evaluation effort to reach convergence. This paper introduces the SPGP-SARL algorithm, which replaces those transitions with greedy actions derived from the current policy rather than chance. This modification accelerates validation without altering the learned strategy. Experiments conducted in an underwater navigation environment confirm that this approach is practical and validates the strategy more rapidly compared to the original methodology.

This paper presents the core components of a computational code designed for two-fluid stellar models within the framework of general relativity in spherical symmetry. It also notes that in cases where the code handles standard (single-fluid) stellar models, the capacity to solve multi-fluid solutions arises directly through its compatibility with single-fluid solutions. The approach numerically solves the Einstein and hydrodynamic equations of motion by employing a finite-difference method alongside a relaxation technique designed to minimize the time evolution equations. The paper concludes by reporting the outcomes obtained when applying the code to the calculation of hydrostatic equilibrium states in relativistic stars.

We introduce a new multi-Task extension for end-to-end neural end-to-TTS (eGEC) adaptation that enhances both end-to-TLS and neural language modeling across multiple tasks simultaneously. Our framework employs a novel dynamic adaptive mechanism to automatically adjust the cross-task transfer intensity for each specific adaptation scenario. By integrating flexible, task-specific adaptive connections, our method achieves superior generalization compared to traditional multi-Task transfer learning approaches, even when only a small number of cross-adaptation tasks are used. Experiments conducted on the English-Wikis and Chinese FGC datasets demonstrate significant improvements in character-level encoding and generation quality compared to single-Task baseline methods.

The HI absorption spectra for 211 HII regions in UGC 8839 have been analyzed to determine their line-of-sight velocity dispersions. When comparing HII region populations at similar radial distances, UGC 8839 exhibits broader median distributions than other spiral galaxies, a trend that also holds true for individual measurements of the dispersion. Furthermore, the mean HII region cluster sizes in UGC 8839 are notably larger, a characteristic linked to elevated stellar formation rates and, consequently, more extensive stellar populations. Regarding the relationship between HII region age and location, UGC 8839 aligns with other galaxies in showing older populations at greater radii. However, its broad median distribution suggests that, for UGC 8839, the influence of galactocentric radius on this broadening effect surpasses the impact seen in other systems. This phenomenon may stem from an unusually high rate of recent star formation or an elevated stellar velocity dispersion, potentially resulting from the latter. Such an outcome could be connected to the galaxy's warped and irregular morphology, which might facilitate the accretion of high-velocity gas.

We analyze multiband optical light variations for the classical T Tauri star V4046 Sagittarii, spanning 14 years of observations from collections by Olofsson et al. (2017) and the current research. The extensive dataset from V4046 Sgr reveals an accretion rate variability spanning more than four orders of magnitude. The paper's recorded spectral energy distribution indicates that the outer disk regions remain depleted throughout the entire timeseries, with only the stellar surface and inner disk regions reflecting these changes in accretion dynamics. Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MAREL) presents a challenging yet promising domain, as it risks the offline data redundancy caused by online exploration. Recent advances in trajectories-as- papers (SIT) has emerged, offering a framework to leverage shared trajectories for offline multi-agent settings by focusing training efforts on demonstrated successful path while distributing credit among all agents involved. This approach inherently prioritizes reusing common trajectories containing multiple abundant, high-quality experiences, thereby facilitating more efficient learning from stored data. In this work, we propose State-Transition Trajectories (SIT)-DQN, an algorithm designed to unlock the full potential of traditional offline multi-agent success stories by targeting these informative common paths. Empirical evaluations across standard benchmarks demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses baseline algorithms in both individual performance and collective return rates.

We recently introduced a bidimensional neural network (2CNN) designed to perform image registration by learning the mapping between convolutonal filters and a fully connected feedforward network. Rather than relying on traditional registration cost functions, this learning approach utilizes the actual identity of objects contained in the images. Training occurs in two phases: initially, the 2Cnn acquires a collection of convolutional filters and control parameters through unsupervised learning; subsequently, these components are refined via supervised feedback derived from gradient calculations of a bolder cost function—specifically, the root-mean-squares error (RMS) between the deformed moving images and the stationary images.

In contrast to conventional CNN approaches that depend on image intensity, our method is grounded in the semantic information of the registered scenes. Consequently, convolutonal patterns evolve to detect structural similarities, while the fully connected layer automatically learns to minimize the registration cost function utilizing this detected information. Experiments confirm that this learned cost function is far more sensitive to registration quality than standard gradient vector field (GVC) metrics, enabling significantly higher registration quality when combined with a gradient descent optimization algorithm.

Specifically, sufficient conditions for their existence are established, hinging on the number of particles, the depth of squeezing, and the extent of phase space nonclassicality. Additionally, a minimum particle count for single-mode EPR steering and spatially separated multi-particle entanglement is determined, given a specific level of squeezing and nonclassicality. Our findings have significant implications for quantum-enhanced sensing networks, cryptography, and the efficient use of resources in future quantum communication systems.

This work introduces a feedback encoding approach designed to lower pilot overhead while preserving the efficiency of Lloyd clustering. Unlike traditional methods, which require extensive pilot signals for learners to report cluster centers, our proposed scheme utilizes overhead-free open standards for feedback encoding. Furthermore, it refines the concept of cluster centers by defining a "cluster representative," which is the minimum-station-cost clustering option passing through an integer-aligned cluster. These independent near-optimal configurations ensure the feedback itself offers encoding gains beyond standard deviations from the mean. Combined, these concepts significantly reduce overhead in large networks and seamlessly integrate with conventional Lloyd algorithms without complicating their structure. Experimental results indicate that per-bit classification cost improves drastically—by more than 240\% in extensive networks—compared to traditional approaches.

This study presents the concept of surface currents, a novel indicator of robustness applicable to both bosonic and fermonic systems, complementing existing surface topological numbers for bosons and surface Fermi arcs for fermions. Surface currents emerge in semi-infinite bosonic and fermionic systems characterized by significant gapping in the bulk spectrum, yet remain absent of spectrum gaps at the interface. Similar to other topological features, these current-induced boundaries display immunity to certain types of perturbations and precise quantification schemes have been developed for both bosonic and fermionic cases. Furthermore, multiple realistic examples demonstrating the emergence of surface currents in both categories of particles are examined. Ultimately, we establish that surface currents originate from the interplay between boundary-induced symmetry breaking and the specific details of system geometry.

This study investigates the physical-layer security (PLS) of an interference network where two information-transmitting nodes and two eavesdroppers coexist with two legitimate receivers. Each transmitter splits its power between a secure message and an intelligent interference intended to constrain eavesdropping, whereas intercepted intelligent interference by recipients is managed via decoding. To evaluate PLS performance and the impact of power distribution strategies, two non-cooperative game models are formulated: a comprehensive game where both nodes choose power allocations for safe data versus clever interference, and a hierarchical game in which nodes sequentially decide, with each subsequent node aware of the prior node's selection. In both games, the safe data rates for recipients and the information rates for eavesdroppers function as utilities, allowing the application of game-theoretic methods to identify equilibria. Specifically, the Nash Equilibrium (NE) resolves the comprehensive game, while a Minimax (MM) approach identifies optimal choices within the hierarchical framework. The identified equilibria and optimals are compared against scenarios where no intelligent interference is employed, highlighting how varying allocation strategies influence total network security.

Text games present an increasingly viable option for NLP model pre-training by offering a dense, cost-effective source of textual data. These games simulate text worlds through agent interactions via textual actions and observations, enabling infinite data generation with an initial setup cost. However, the extensive search space required to explore these environments has historically hindered large-scale exploration. Previously, TextWorld training involved an manual curriculum; last month, our TextWorldExpress automatically curated a similar path, contracting the curricular curriculum by 96% while exploring a broader diversity of states and edges. Currently, TextWorldExpress is open-sourcing the curriculum and an observation function specific to Pegasus, which is crucial for enhancing the volume and variety of the simulated dataset. In this work, we assess the impact of this dataset on intermediate model stages and highlight improvements. Specifically, training an intermediate model using this enhanced human-aligned pretraining curriculum shows that even with the reduced state exploration, the curriculum, when used to pretrain humans, preconditions the model better than standard random conditions for playing the text world games with Pegasus. To support this, we have doubled the game simulation dataset size to 2000 steps per episode, up from 100 steps, and increased state-variety by 1,100 new states compared to an 11% random exploration rate. With this enhanced dataset, conditioned models outperformed the baseline by 0.5 to 1.5 percentage points in 0.

Designing Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) for Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models presents a significant challenge, as these workloads are computationally and data-memory intensive, often causing a mismatch between an application's timing requirements and the available memory bandwidth. While previous designs have relied on area- and power-constrained architectures, they typically suffer from underutilized compute units due to communication bottlenecks. To address this, we propose a novel, high-performance LSTM processor architecture based on a hybrid FPGA distributed memory and shared memory (FDHT) paired with an LSTM-specific LSTM architecture. This proposed FDHT combined with LSTM-specific shared time-memory architecture (FDHT-LSTM) significantly improves data throughput, computational efficiency, and memory bandwidth. The FDHT-LSTM design has been evaluated for an image segmentation task using the Microsoft COCO dataset and compared against existing models, including a traditional, area-efficient, tensor-based decomposed architecture. The FDHL-LSTM model has been selected for extensive use in the image segmentation task due to its superior performance metrics, such as higher data throughput, computational efficiency, and memory bandwidth. Simulation results indicate that the proposed FDHT-LSTM design delivers a 2.33× increase in data throughput, a 1.47× improvement in computational efficiency, and a 1.41× improvement in memory bandwidth compared to the baseline.

A new variant of the Weak Gravity Conjecture (WGC) is introduced specifically for theories containing a cosmological constant in anti-de Sitter (dS) contexts. This paper investigates challenges in multi-domain physics simulation, where an environment may encompass multiple distinct tasks or entire libraries of environments, each requiring its own dynamics model. We focus on multi-environment reinforcement learning (RETL), a setting where an agent learns within various environments, potentially under different settings, without access to their specific dynamics or the task of identifying environment memberships. Recognizing auditory scenes is vital for enhancing human-computer interaction and ensuring safety in autonomous vehicles. Currently, the field relies on the VGG-Sound (VGG-SS) benchmark, which includes 1.5 million clips of two classes (tools and household items) drawn from larger datasets. To address this limitation, we introduce VGGSoundBERT, a benchmark that provides extensive audio-visual pairs for the "tools" category. Our dataset offers synchronized videos with action labels, 9 seconds of video-per-clip, 14,000 video-kilometers labeled with text captions, and a content license permitting self-supervised pretraining. We introduce AudioCLIP, a model trained on this new benchmark using AudioCLiP for clips, BERT for text, and VGG for images. Results indicate that utilizing visual information boosts accuracy by 8%, rising from 76% to 84%. Furthermore, our analysis reveals limited diversity among content, voiceover, and speaker sources, and we show how visual auxiliary information enhances cross-modal transfer learning performance significantly.

Our key innovation involves a novel contraction operator that aggregates geometric information specifically tailored to the relationships between nodes and triangles. Crucially, LGCN functions independently of the particular element-centric representations currently in use and demonstrates superior node classification outcomes compared to state-of-the-art hyperbolic GCNs on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Moreover, because it relies directly on the input-output mapping of standard GCNs, it can be integrated as a modular component into various architecture frameworks.

The emergence of power-law statistics in social systems like urban growth can be understood through the Tsallis distribution ($q$-exponential), derived via the principle of maximum entropy under specific constraints. This study formulates a model for rank-based population growth—where a city's growth rate correlates with its current size—by constructing an energy-like "pension" function dependent on population rank. Furthermore, the model demonstrates how a subtle, rank-proportionate growth mechanism allows macro-level power laws to arise from simple rules, without necessitating complex many-body interactions or critical phenomena, challenging the view that such patterns are universal indicators of deep, hidden system dynamics.

D97, 115009 (2018)], dark parity emerged as unavoidable in this setup if the dark sector is assumed to be minimal. However, we now question this minimality. Instead, we propose a non-Abelian dark gauge theory featuring fermions in a self-interacting potential designed to stabilize the vacuum and prevent tachyonic modes post-electroweak symmetry breaking. We demonstrate that these elements inevitably break dark parity at the Seesaw scale and raise issues concerning the unitary limit of the dark sector's scattering amplitudes at accessible energies. Conversely, an Abelian dark sector is shown to be consistent with all constraints, requiring only a stable hierarchy between the dark and visible sectors to preserve the symmetry.

Spin-orbit coupling (SOC) in transition metal (TM) oxides presents a tunable energy scale that rivals both the fundamental electronic interactions and the crystal field splitting. When SOC reaches this intermediate regime, the resulting rich and diverse physics is best explored through the Schrieffer–Wolff (SW) decoupling approach. However, employing SW requires an explicit definition of the active subspace, particularly concerning the filled and empty orbital states relative to the chemical bonds formed between cations and anions. This article utilizes DFT+U calculations to examine how the choice of orbital subspace influences the effective low-energy model derived via SW decoupling, focusing on Ti and iridium (Ir) compounds. By analyzing the SW parameters across varying distributions of d-orbitals, we identify that the apparent interaction and SOC strengths within the reduced low-energy model are highly sensitive to subspace selection, even after accounting for the crystal field split. Specifically, we demonstrate distinct SW outcomes for diagonal versus off-diagonal configurations of the crystal field, both within and outside the presence of chemical bonding effects.

This paper derives a precise formula expressing the complete intersection of toric varieties in terms of a complete toric subdivision. It demonstrates that a smooth toric complete intersection, when its complete subvariety is removed, yields a complete toric partition with a weighted complete intersection that is completely subvaritized. This complete subdivision can be represented as a linear transformation of the original complete subdivision, with a weighting system derived from the original complete subdivision and subvariety. This result generalizes the finding presented by Tseng and Yu (2009), which previously addressed only toric blowups, to encompass all toric complete intersections.

Diagnosing rare diseases often proves difficult due to limited data for training medical AI models. Generative technology addresses this challenge by augmenting AI: first, synthetic images and labels are created to enhance sparse datasets containing actual case labels; subsequently, reverse generative models convert these new fake images into labels based on the original synthetic labels. This process relies on adjusting latent space representations to render images depicting specific rare conditions. However, current methods struggle when dealing with conditions that are genuinely rare in the source data, resulting in generated images of poor quality that offer limited diagnostic value. We introduce a method to mitigate this by training entirely new generative models dedicated to each rare condition, allowing for effective manipulation of its specific latent representation to produce images accurately labeled with the targeted rare disease. Empirical results demonstrate a notable improvement over baseline approaches using real-world datasets across multiple isolated class-conditional image generation tasks.
